newsitem.title: UK: British peer to challenge royal succession rule.
newsitem.headline: British peer to challenge royal succession rule.

text.p: Lord Archer, prominent Conservative party peer and best-selling novelist, wants to change an ancient constitutional rule which puts men above women in the line of succession to the British throne.

Jeffrey Archer, as he is best known to his wide readership, is taking legal advice on how to draw up a bill to change the rule -- known as the law of primogeniture -- that the monarch's eldest child only succeeds if he is male.
A daughter can only succeed to the throne if, like Queen Elizabeth, she has no brothers.
Any change would have little effect for at least two more generations. Prince Charles, the queen's eldest son, is heir to the throne. His elder son, William, would succeed him.

But Archer, a former Conservative member of the House of Commons (lower house of parliament) now sitting in the House of Lords (upper house), said: "My attitude is, let's change the law now so that if we produce another Elizabeth in 70 years we can put her on the throne," he told a BBC interviewer.
A House of Lords official said the rules on succession were part of Britain's largely unwritten constitution but could be altered by a law passed by parliament.
Archer said he believed there was support for the idea from the queen, who herself became sovereign through a quirk of history.
The crown passed to her father, the second son of George V, after her uncle Edward renounced the throne to marry American divorcee Wallis Simpson.
Elizabeth, the elder of two daughters, became sovereign when her father, then King George VI, died in 1952.

Senior members of the royal family, whose public image has been battered by marital problems among the Queen's children, held talks behind closed doors in August on how to adapt the monarchy to ensure its survival into the next century.

Royal watchers speculated that the law of succession was one of the subjects discussed. But Buckingham Palace said on Tuesday that the idea for Archer's initiative had not come from the royal family and it was for parliament to make its views known.
Prime Minister John Major's Conservative administration also declined to comment on the initiative on Tuesday.
A spokesman said the government had not seen the bill and would consider it only after studying any proposals for change.
But there would be problems getting the bill through the Lords, parliament's upper chamber.
Two years ago, Britain's peers threw out an attempt to change the rule laying down that hereditary titles are passed down the male side of the family.
